--- title: "Einführung in R und Quarto" subtitle: "Int_R_oduction" author: "Andreas Haupt" bibliography: IntRo.bib format: revealjs: theme: style.scss css: global.css slideNumber: true fig-align: center editor: source execute: echo: true message: false warning: false --- ## What you will learn ![*Source*: Saskia Otto, Uni Hamburg](https://mareds.github.io/r_course/img_site/Tidyverse_packages.png) ## Workflow 1. Use **Projects** to manage all files (scripts, data, figures and tables) belonging to the same project. 2. Use the editor the write **scripts**, so you can reproduce your results. ## Set up your "IntRo" project - Set up a new project in . + "New Directory" + "New Project" + Finally, a name for the folder and under "Browse" where you want that folder to be located. + **Done!** Now you should find an empty folder under the path your wanted it to be set up. + In the future, start Positron by double clicking on the project icon in your folder. ## First steps with R — Creating **objects** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # I am a comment; the hashtag "#" makes me one. # It is good programming style to use me a lot ;). ``` ::: . . . R is an _**object**-oriented_ programming language. We create objects with the **assignment operator** `<-`.
::: {.note} The names you give objects need to start with a letter. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a new object "test_object" and assign to it the result of 5 + 2 test_object <- 5 + 2 ``` ::: . . . The assignment operator may be used in both *directions*: `<-`, or `->`. ::: {.note} This can help you write more legible code. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 5 + 3 -> another_test_object # Create another object ``` ::: ## First steps with R — Creating **objects** Objects can contain all kinds of information. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} text_object <- "Yes, you can also assign text" ``` ::: ## First steps with R — Printing objects You can make R print the content of an object by typing its name. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_object # Print object ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} another_test_object ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} text_object ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Yes, you can also assign text" ``` ::: ::: ## Printing $\neq$ assigning! If you don't use the assignment operator, R will simply print the result of an operation without changing that object (i.e., without any further consequences). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_object + 3 # Print the result of adding 3 to the content of test_object + 3. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} test_object # Print the content of test_object. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7 ``` ::: ::: ## Printing $\neq$ assigning! If you actually want to create or modify objects, you need to use the assignment operator and explicitly assign the result of your operation to the object you want to change. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_object <- test_object + 3 # Assign to test_object: the result of adding 3 to the content of test_object. test_object # Print the content of test_object ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 ``` ::: ::: The short-hand version for assigning and printing an object right away uses surrounding `()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (test_object <- 5 + 2) # Assign the result of 5 + 2 to "test_object" and print tat object's content. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7 ``` ::: ::: ## First steps with R — **Functions** Functions do the work in R. You call/use them by:
` function_name(argument1 = value1, argument2 = value2, ...)` The `seq()` function, for instance, produces a sequence of numbers and has (among others) the arguments `from` and `to`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (yet_another_object <- seq(from = 1, to = 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ::: ## Printing $\neq$ assigning! To shorten code, R can infer the arguments by their position (i.e., the positions of supplied values).
::: {.note} (i.e., Here R assumes you mean from-to and *not* to-from) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (yet_another_object <- seq(1, 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ::: ## First steps with R — Object **classes** What a function does, depends on the type of object you feed to its arguments as values. The `class()` function tells you what **class**/type of object your are dealing with: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(yet_another_object) # "yet_another_object" contails whole numbers, so it is: ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(text_object) # "text_object" contains a sentence, so it is: ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: ## First steps with R — Object **classes** Functions will throw an error message, if you feed them with an object of a class it cannot handle: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} alphabet <- seq(from = "a", to = "z") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `seq.default()`: ! 'from' must be a finite number ``` ::: ::: . . . Although functions do stuff with objects we feed to them, they are also objects themselves: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(seq) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "function" ``` ::: ::: ## **Arithmetic operators** Like any decent calculator, R knows how to handle basic arithmetic: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 2 + 3 # Plus ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 2 - 3 # Minus ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 2 * 3 # Multiplication ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 2 / 3 # Devision ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6666667 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 2^3 # Power ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ::: . . . Other mathematical operations are implemented as functions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yet_another_object # Print another_object. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sqrt(yet_another_object) # Print square root of every element contained in another_object. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.000000 1.414214 1.732051 2.000000 2.236068 ``` ::: ::: ## **Logical** (Boolean) **operators** ::: {.centered} `&` "and", `|` "or", and `!` "not" ::: ![](https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/01f4b6d39d2be8269740a3ad7946faa79f7243cf/8369a/diagrams/transform-logical.png){width="80%"} ::: {.centered} ::: {.note} *Source*: Wickham & Grolemund [R for Data Science](http://r4ds.had.co.nz/transform.html) ::: ::: ## Logical (Boolean) operators — In action ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 2 # Assign 2 to object x x == 3 # equals ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x != 3 # unequals ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x < 5 # less than ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x > 5 # greater than ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <= 5 # less or equal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x >= 2 # greater or equal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x > 5 & 6 # greater than 5 and greater than 6 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x > 5 | 1 # greater than 5 or greater then 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x >= (5 & 6) | (5 & 1) | (1 & 2) # Complex comparison ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ## Getting **help** R has a steep learning curve and is, at times, simply frustrating. The documentation of a specific function can be accessed via typing `?`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ?seq() ``` ::: You can find further useful links on the course website. ## Today's general lessons 1. R is an **object**-oriented programming language. Objects are basically containers and they can contain anything: data, functions, other objects, results, figures, and more ... Objects can be called by their name, which needs to start with a letter. If you just type the name of an object, R prints the object. 2. **Functions** do stuff with objects, which we assign as **values** to a function's **arguments**. What exactly a function does, depends on the **class** of an object. Functions themselves are objects too. ## Operators 1. `?`: View a function's help file. 2. `#`: defines a **comment** in your code. Comment as much as possible! 3. `<-`: is the **assignment operator** of R. It creates objects and assigns information to them. 4. `->`: is the **reversed assignment operator** of R. It also creates objects and assigns information to them. 5. `+`, `-`, `*`, `\`, `^` : **Arithmetic operators** 6. `&` "and", `|` "or", `!` "not" : **Logical** (Boolean) **operators** ## Today's (important) functions 1. `class()`: tells you the class of an object. ## Literatur ::: {#refs} :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
